facts.fact_text: On 9 January 2002, the parliamentary group of the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) held a gathering in Great National Assembly Square, in front of government headquarters.
The parliamentary group of the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) also held gatherings on 11, 13, 15, 16 and 17 January 2002.
The participants in the gatherings shown in the video appeared to number several hundred and included people of different ages varying from schoolchildren to pensioners.
No signs of violence can be seen in the video submitted by the Government of the gatherings held on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.

On 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice issued an official warning to the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) in accordance with section 27 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991.

In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice stated that the CDPP had breached the provisions of section 6 of the Assemblies Act by organising demonstrations in Great National Assembly Square on 9, 10, 11 and 13 January 2002.

In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice stated that the CDPP had organised demonstrations in Great National Assembly Square notwithstanding that the authorisation issued by Chișinău Municipal Council only gave permission for a demonstration on 9 January 2002 in National Opera Square.
In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice called for an immediate halt to the gatherings, which it considered to be illegal and unconstitutional.

In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice claimed that the gatherings were not meetings with voters within the meaning of the Status of Members of Parliament Act, but demonstrations falling under the Assemblies Act.
In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice asked the CDPP for a written explanation within three days.

In its warning of 14 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice warned the CDPP that if it failed to comply with the warning, the Ministry would impose a temporary ban (suspendarea activităţii) on the party's activities in accordance with section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act.

On 18 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice issued a decision imposing a one-month ban on the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP)'s activities, in accordance with section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991.
The one-month ban on the CDPP's activities imposed on 18 January 2002 was based on the organisation by the CDPP of unauthorised demonstrations on 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16 and 17 January 2002.
The Ministry of Justice dismissed the CDPP leader's argument that the party could not be held liable for the gatherings organised by its parliamentary group.

In its decision of 18 January 2002, the Ministry of Justice stated that the gatherings organised by the CDPP on 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16 and 17 January 2002 had in fact been demonstrations and marches and therefore fell within the scope of the Assemblies Act rather than the Status of Members of Parliament Act.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the CDPP had breached the provisions of sections 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 11 of the Assemblies Act by not obtaining prior authorisation from Chișinău Municipal Council to stage demonstrations.
According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the CDPP had breached the provisions of sections 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 11 of the Assemblies Act by blocking the public highway.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the participation of minors in the CDPP demonstrations had been in breach of Article 15 of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child of 20 November 1989.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the participation of minors in the CDPP demonstrations had been in breach of section 13(3) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994.
According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the participation of minors in the CDPP demonstrations had been in breach of section 56(g) of the Education Act of 21 July 1995.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the CDPP's actions disclosed a violation of sections 27 and 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991.
According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the CDPP's actions disclosed a violation of section 15(1) and (2) of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994.
According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the CDPP's actions disclosed a violation of Article 32 of the Constitution of the Republic of Moldova.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the use of the slogan 'I'd rather be dead than a communist' (Mai bine mort decât comunist) could be interpreted as a call to public violence and an act undermining the legal and constitutional order.
On 24 January 2002, the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) challenged the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002 imposing a one-month ban on its activities.

In its challenge of 24 January 2002, the CDPP argued, inter alia, that the gatherings had been meetings with voters within the meaning of the Status of Members of Parliament Act, and not assemblies falling within the scope of the Assemblies Act.
On 8 February 2002, the Ministry of Justice issued a decision lifting the temporary ban imposed on the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP)'s activities.

In its decision of 8 February 2002, the Ministry of Justice stressed that the CDPP had breached all the laws mentioned in the decision of 18 January 2002 and that the temporary ban had been necessary and justified.
The Ministry of Justice lifted the temporary ban on the CDPP's activities following an inquiry by the Secretary General of the Council of Europe under Article 52 of the Convention.
The Ministry of Justice lifted the temporary ban on the CDPP's activities having regard to the forthcoming local elections.
The Ministry of Justice's decision of 8 February 2002 lifting the temporary ban did not set aside the decision of 18 January 2002 imposing the ban.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal of the Republic of Moldova found in favour of the Ministry of Justice and ruled that the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002 imposing a one-month ban on the CDPP's activities had been lawful.
On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal dismissed the CDPP's argument that the party could not be held liable for the actions of its members, namely its parliamentary group.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal found that the gatherings organised by the CDPP had in fact been demonstrations, meetings and marches which fell under the provisions of the Assemblies Act, and not meetings with voters.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal found that even assuming the gatherings had been intended as meetings with voters, they had gradually taken on the nature of demonstrations and, accordingly, the CDPP needed authorisation in order to organise them.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal stated that as a result of the CDPP demonstrations, the public transport company had suffered losses of 12,133 Moldovan lei (MDL), equivalent to approximately 1,050 euros (EUR) at the time.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal found that the participation of minors in the CDPP demonstrations had been in breach of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child of 20 November 1989, the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 and the Education Act of 21 July 1995.
The Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) lodged an appeal against the Court of Appeal's decision of 7 March 2002 with the Supreme Court of Justice of the Republic of Moldova.
In its appeal to the Supreme Court of Justice, the CDPP relied, inter alia, on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention.

On 17 May 2002, a panel of the Supreme Court of Justice of the Republic of Moldova delivered its judgment dismissing the appeal lodged by the CDPP against the Court of Appeal's decision of 7 March 2002.
In its judgment of 17 May 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice endorsed the arguments of the Court of Appeal.
In its judgment of 17 May 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice found that since the demonstrations organised by the CDPP had been illegal, the sanction imposed on it had not been disproportionate.

In its judgment of 17 May 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice stated that in any event the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002 had not had any negative effects on the CDPP since it had not been enforced, the CDPP's accounts had not been frozen and the party could continue its activities unhindered.
The Ministry of Justice did not reply to Chișinău Municipal Council's request of 23 January 2002 for interpretation of the law.
The Ministry of Justice did not address any request to Parliament for an official interpretation of the legislation, as requested by Chișinău Municipal Council on 23 January 2002.

On 21 February 2002, the government of the Republic of Moldova lodged an application with the Supreme Court of Justice asking it, inter alia, to declare the demonstrations organised by the CDPP illegal and to order their cessation.
On 25 February 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice ruled in favour of the government and declared the CDPP gatherings illegal.

In its ruling of 25 February 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice stated that even if the CDPP had the initial intention of holding meetings with its supporters, those meetings later took on the character of demonstrations, marches, processions and picketing, which fall under the provisions of the Assemblies Act, and that the leaders of the CDPP were therefore required to comply with the provisions of the Assemblies Act.
The Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) appealed against the Supreme Court of Justice's ruling of 25 February 2002.
On 15 March 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice dismissed the CDPP's appeal against the ruling of 25 February 2002.
The Supreme Court of Justice's judgment of 25 February 2002 declaring the CDPP gatherings illegal became final on 15 March 2002.
In the course of the present proceedings before the Court, the Government submitted a video with images of gatherings held by CDPP deputies on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.
The gatherings shown in the video submitted by the Government were held in Great National Assembly Square, in a pedestrian area, in front of the government buildings.
The participants in the gatherings shown in the video appeared to number several hundred and included people of different ages varying from schoolchildren to pensioners.
According to the time displayed on the video images, the gatherings commenced at around 1 p.m. and lasted for about two hours.
During the gatherings shown in the video, different personalities made speeches critical of the ruling Communist Party, the government and its policy.
It appears from the video submitted by the Government that traffic was not disrupted as a result of the gatherings held on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.
No signs of violence can be seen in the video submitted by the Government of the gatherings held on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.
'The Layabout's Anthem' (Imnul Golanilor — a song that originated in the 1990 Bucharest student demonstrations) was played frequently at the gatherings shown in the video.

The chorus of 'The Layabout's Anthem' (Imnul Golanilor) included the following lines: 'I'd rather be a slacker than a traitor (Mai bine haimana, decât trădător) / I'd rather be a hooligan than a dictator (Mai bine huligan, decât dictator) / I'd rather be a layabout than an activist (Mai bine golan, decât activist) / I'd rather be dead than a communist (Mai bine mort, decât comunist).'

Article 32(3) of the Constitution of the Republic of Moldova provides that denial and defamation of the State and of the people, incitement to war of aggression, incitement to hatred on ethnic, racial or religious grounds, incitement to discrimination, territorial separatism or public violence, as well as other acts undermining the constitutional order shall be forbidden and shall be punishable under the law.

Section 15(1) of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994 provides that members of parliament shall be obliged strictly to observe the Constitution, the laws and the rules of morality and ethics.

Section 15(2) of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994 provides that members of parliament shall have a duty to be dependable and to contribute by their own example to the consolidation of State discipline, the fulfilment of civil obligations, the protection of human rights and the observance of the law.

Section 15(3) of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994 provides that alleged breaches of the rules of ethics by members of parliament shall be examined by the Parliamentary Commission on Legal Affairs, Appointments and Immunity.

Section 22(3) of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994 (as originally enacted) provides that local authorities shall provide members of parliament with all necessary assistance for the organisation of their work with voters and shall place premises at their disposal for meetings with voters.

On 26 July 2002, section 22(3) of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994 was amended to provide that local authorities shall provide members of parliament with the necessary assistance for the organisation of their work with voters, shall ensure access to buildings or other public places, provide equipment and any necessary information, and inform voters in good time about the place and time of meetings with members of parliament.

On 26 July 2002, a new section 22(1) was introduced into the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994, providing that members of parliament shall have the right to organise demonstrations, meetings, processions and other peaceful gatherings in accordance with the Assemblies Act.

Section 23(1) of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994 provides that members of parliament, in their capacity as representatives of the supreme legislative power, shall have the right to raise demands on the spot for action to remedy a breach of the law.
Section 5 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted only after the organisers have notified the local council.

Section 6(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be conducted peacefully, without any sort of weapons, and shall ensure the protection of participants and the environment, without impeding the normal use of public highways, road traffic and the operation of economic undertakings and without degenerating into acts of violence capable of endangering the public order and the physical integrity and life of persons or their property.
On 26 July 2002, a new section 6(2) was added to the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995, providing that teachers or other school staff members shall not involve students in unauthorised assemblies.

Section 7 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be suspended in circumstances including: denial and defamation of the State and of the people; incitement to war of aggression and incitement to hatred on ethnic, racial or religious grounds; incitement to discrimination, territorial separatism or public violence; and acts that undermine the constitutional order.

Section 8(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted in squares, streets, parks and other public places in cities, towns and villages, and also in public buildings.

Section 8(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct an assembly in the buildings of the public authorities, the local authorities, prosecutors' offices, the courts or companies with armed security.

Section 8(3)(a) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within fifty metres of the parliament building, the residence of the President of Moldova, the seat of the government, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of Justice.

Section 8(3)(b) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within twenty-five metres of the buildings of the central administrative authority, the local public authorities, courts, prosecutors' offices, police stations, prisons and social rehabilitation institutions, military installations, railway stations, airports, hospitals, companies which use dangerous equipment and machines, and diplomatic institutions.
Section 8(4) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that free access to the premises of the institutions listed in section 8(3) shall be guaranteed.
Section 8(5) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local public authorities may, if the organisers agree, establish places or buildings for permanent assemblies.
Section 9 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the date and time of the assembly shall be agreed by the organiser and the local council of the city, town or village.
Section 11(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that not later than fifteen days prior to the date of the assembly, the organiser shall submit a notification to the Municipal Council.

Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate: the name of the organiser and the aim of the assembly; the date, starting time and finishing time; the location and the access and return routes; the manner in which the assembly is to take place; the approximate number of participants; the persons who are to ensure and answer for the sound conduct of the assembly; and the services the organiser asks the Municipal Council to provide.

Section 11(3) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that if the situation so requires, the Municipal Council may alter certain aspects of the prior notification with the agreement of the organiser of the assembly.

Section 12(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that when the prior notification is considered at an ordinary or extraordinary meeting of the Municipal Council, the discussion shall deal with the form, timetable, location and other conditions for the conduct of the assembly and the decision taken shall take account of the specific situation.

Section 27 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991 provides that in the event that breaches of the statute or of the law are discovered in the activities of a party or a socio-political organisation, the Ministry of Justice shall warn its leaders in writing, requesting that the breaches be remedied within a fixed time-limit.

Section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991 (as originally enacted) provides that the Ministry of Justice shall impose a temporary ban on the activities of a party or socio-political organisation which breaches the provisions of the Constitution or those of the Act, or does not comply with a warning.

On 21 November 2003, section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act of 17 September 1991 was amended to provide that the Ministry of Justice shall impose a temporary ban on the activities of a party or socio-political organisation which breaches the provisions of the Constitution, and shall inform the party's leadership in writing of the breaches and set a time-limit for remedying them.

The amended section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act (as amended on 21 November 2003) provides that during electoral campaigns the activities of parties and other socio-political organisations may be suspended only by the Supreme Court of Justice.

The amended section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act (as amended on 21 November 2003) provides that during the temporary ban, it shall be forbidden for the party to use the mass media, to disseminate propaganda and publicity, to carry out bank transactions or other operations in respect of its assets and to participate in elections.

The amended section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act (as amended on 21 November 2003) provides that once all the breaches of the law have been remedied, the party shall inform the Ministry of Justice, which shall lift the temporary ban within five days.

The amended section 29 of the Parties and other Socio-Political Organisations Act (as amended on 21 November 2003) provides that the activities of the party or other socio-political organisation may be suspended for a period of up to six months, and if the breaches of the law are not remedied, for a period of one year.

Article 15(1) of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child of 20 November 1989 provides that States Parties recognise the rights of the child to freedom of association and to freedom of peaceful assembly.

Article 15(2) of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child of 20 November 1989 provides that no restrictions may be placed on the exercise of children's rights to freedom of association and peaceful assembly other than those imposed in conformity with the law and which are necessary in a democratic society in the interests of national security or public safety, public order (ordre public), the protection of public health or morals or the protection of the rights and freedoms of others.
Section 13(1) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 provides that children shall have the right to membership of non-governmental organisations in accordance with the law.

Section 13(2) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 provides that the State must provide children's non-governmental organisations with financial support, place premises at their disposal and provide them with fiscal incentives.
Section 13(3) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 provides that the involvement of children in politics and their membership of political parties shall be forbidden.
Section 56(g) of the Education Act of 21 July 1995 provides that it shall be the duty of teachers not to involve children in street actions (meetings, demonstrations, picketing, etc.).

Article 174(1)(2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 29 March 1985 provides that the organisation and holding of an assembly without prior notification to the Municipal Council or without authorisation from the Council, or in breach of the conditions concerning the conduct of meetings indicated in the authorisation, shall be punishable by a fine imposed on the organisers (leaders) of the assembly in an amount equal to between ten and twenty-five times the minimum monthly wage.

Article 174(1)(4) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 29 March 1985 provides that active participation in an assembly organised without prior notification or authorisation shall be punishable by a fine of between 180 and 450 Moldovan lei (MDL).

On 26 July 2002, a new provision (Article 174(1)(7)) was added to the Code of Administrative Offences of 29 March 1985, providing that the involvement of children in unauthorised assemblies shall be punishable by a fine of between 180 and 360 Moldovan lei (MDL).

The CDPP parliamentary group relied on section 22 of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994, arguing that it did not require members of parliament to obtain prior authorisation for meetings with their supporters.

By a decision of 3 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council classified the gathering to be held on 9 January 2002 as a 'demonstration' within the meaning of sections 4, 8, 12 and 13 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995.

By a decision of 3 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council authorised the parliamentary group of the Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) to hold the gathering on 9 January 2002 in National Opera Square rather than Great National Assembly Square.
Chișinău Municipal Council's decision of 3 January 2002 did not give any reasons for the change of location from Great National Assembly Square to National Opera Square.

On 23 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council addressed a letter to the Ministry of Justice informing it that there was a discrepancy between the provisions of the Status of Members of Parliament Act and those of the Assemblies Act.

In its letter of 23 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council informed the Ministry of Justice that it did not know which of the two Acts — the Status of Members of Parliament Act or the Assemblies Act — to apply.

In its letter of 23 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council stated that a number of reputable lawyers supported the idea that CDPP members of parliament had the right to hold meetings with their supporters in Great National Assembly Square without obtaining prior authorisation, in accordance with sections 22 and 23 of the Status of Members of Parliament Act.

In its letter of 23 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council cited the opinion of an ombudsman who considered that, since section 23 of the Status of Members of Parliament Act proclaimed the right of members of parliament to raise demands on the spot for action to remedy a breach of the law, the CDPP members of parliament were entitled to raise their demands for the cessation of the alleged breaches concerning the introduction of compulsory Russian lessons in front of the government building.
The ombudsman's opinion noted that the government building also housed the Ministry of Education, which was relevant to the CDPP members of parliament's right to raise demands there.
In its letter of 23 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council requested the Ministry of Justice to ask Parliament for an official interpretation of the legislation in question.

On 26 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council issued a decision noting that the provisions of domestic legislation were contradictory in respect of the demonstrations organised by the CDPP and that the opinions of legal experts were contradictory.
In its decision of 26 January 2002, Chișinău Municipal Council suspended its decision of 3 January 2002 until Parliament had given its official interpretation of the relevant legislation.

Section 13(1) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 provides that children shall have the right to membership of non-governmental organisations in accordance with the law.

Section 13(2) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 provides that the State must provide children's non-governmental organisations with financial support, place premises at their disposal and provide them with fiscal incentives.
Section 13(3) of the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 provides that the involvement of children in politics and their membership of political parties shall be forbidden.

Article 174(1)(2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 29 March 1985 provides that the organisation and holding of an assembly without prior notification to the Municipal Council or without authorisation from the Council, or in breach of the conditions concerning the conduct of meetings indicated in the authorisation, shall be punishable by a fine imposed on the organisers (leaders) of the assembly in an amount equal to between ten and twenty-five times the minimum monthly wage.

Article 174(1)(4) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 29 March 1985 provides that active participation in an assembly organised without prior notification or authorisation shall be punishable by a fine of between 180 and 450 Moldovan lei (MDL).

Towards the end of 2001, the Moldovan government made public its intention to make the study of the Russian language compulsory in schools for children aged seven and over.
The Moldovan government's initiative to make Russian language study compulsory prompted vehement criticism from the opposition.

Article 32(3) of the Constitution of the Republic of Moldova provides that denial and defamation of the State and of the people, incitement to war of aggression, incitement to hatred on ethnic, racial or religious grounds, incitement to discrimination, territorial separatism or public violence, as well as other acts undermining the constitutional order shall be forbidden and shall be punishable under the law.

Section 15(1) of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994 provides that members of parliament shall be obliged strictly to observe the Constitution, the laws and the rules of morality and ethics.

Section 15(2) of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994 provides that members of parliament shall have a duty to be dependable and to contribute by their own example to the consolidation of State discipline, the fulfilment of civil obligations, the protection of human rights and the observance of the law.

On 26 July 2002, a new section 22(1) was introduced into the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994, providing that members of parliament shall have the right to organise demonstrations, meetings, processions and other peaceful gatherings in accordance with the Assemblies Act.

Section 23(1) of the Status of Members of Parliament Act of 7 April 1994 provides that members of parliament, in their capacity as representatives of the supreme legislative power, shall have the right to raise demands on the spot for action to remedy a breach of the law.
Section 5 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted only after the organisers have notified the local council.

Section 6(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be conducted peacefully, without any sort of weapons, and shall ensure the protection of participants and the environment, without impeding the normal use of public highways, road traffic and the operation of economic undertakings and without degenerating into acts of violence capable of endangering the public order and the physical integrity and life of persons or their property.
On 26 July 2002, a new section 6(2) was added to the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995, providing that teachers or other school staff members shall not involve students in unauthorised assemblies.

Section 7 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be suspended in circumstances including: denial and defamation of the State and of the people; incitement to war of aggression and incitement to hatred on ethnic, racial or religious grounds; incitement to discrimination, territorial separatism or public violence; and acts that undermine the constitutional order.

Section 8(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted in squares, streets, parks and other public places in cities, towns and villages, and also in public buildings.

Section 8(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct an assembly in the buildings of the public authorities, the local authorities, prosecutors' offices, the courts or companies with armed security.

Section 8(3)(a) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within fifty metres of the parliament building, the residence of the President of Moldova, the seat of the government, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of Justice.

Section 8(3)(b) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within twenty-five metres of the buildings of the central administrative authority, the local public authorities, courts, prosecutors' offices, police stations, prisons and social rehabilitation institutions, military installations, railway stations, airports, hospitals, companies which use dangerous equipment and machines, and diplomatic institutions.
Section 8(4) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that free access to the premises of the institutions listed in section 8(3) shall be guaranteed.
Section 8(5) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local public authorities may, if the organisers agree, establish places or buildings for permanent assemblies.
Section 9 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the date and time of the assembly shall be agreed by the organiser and the local council of the city, town or village.
Section 11(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that not later than fifteen days prior to the date of the assembly, the organiser shall submit a notification to the Municipal Council.

Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate: the name of the organiser and the aim of the assembly; the date, starting time and finishing time; the location and the access and return routes; the manner in which the assembly is to take place; the approximate number of participants; the persons who are to ensure and answer for the sound conduct of the assembly; and the services the organiser asks the Municipal Council to provide.

Section 11(3) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that if the situation so requires, the Municipal Council may alter certain aspects of the prior notification with the agreement of the organiser of the assembly.

Section 12(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that when the prior notification is considered at an ordinary or extraordinary meeting of the Municipal Council, the discussion shall deal with the form, timetable, location and other conditions for the conduct of the assembly and the decision taken shall take account of the specific situation.

According to the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002, the use of the slogan 'I'd rather be dead than a communist' (Mai bine mort decât comunist) could be interpreted as a call to public violence and an act undermining the legal and constitutional order.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal stated that as a result of the CDPP demonstrations, the public transport company had suffered losses of 12,133 Moldovan lei (MDL), equivalent to approximately 1,050 euros (EUR) at the time.

On 7 March 2002, the Court of Appeal found that the participation of minors in the CDPP demonstrations had been in breach of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child of 20 November 1989, the Protection of Children Act of 15 December 1994 and the Education Act of 21 July 1995.
The Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) lodged an appeal against the Court of Appeal's decision of 7 March 2002 with the Supreme Court of Justice of the Republic of Moldova.
In its appeal to the Supreme Court of Justice, the CDPP relied, inter alia, on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention.

On 17 May 2002, a panel of the Supreme Court of Justice of the Republic of Moldova delivered its judgment dismissing the appeal lodged by the CDPP against the Court of Appeal's decision of 7 March 2002.
In its judgment of 17 May 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice endorsed the arguments of the Court of Appeal.
In its judgment of 17 May 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice found that since the demonstrations organised by the CDPP had been illegal, the sanction imposed on it had not been disproportionate.

In its judgment of 17 May 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice stated that in any event the Ministry of Justice's decision of 18 January 2002 had not had any negative effects on the CDPP since it had not been enforced, the CDPP's accounts had not been frozen and the party could continue its activities unhindered.
The Ministry of Justice did not reply to Chișinău Municipal Council's request of 23 January 2002 for interpretation of the law.
The Ministry of Justice did not address any request to Parliament for an official interpretation of the legislation, as requested by Chișinău Municipal Council on 23 January 2002.

On 21 February 2002, the government of the Republic of Moldova lodged an application with the Supreme Court of Justice asking it, inter alia, to declare the demonstrations organised by the CDPP illegal and to order their cessation.
On 25 February 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice ruled in favour of the government and declared the CDPP gatherings illegal.

In its ruling of 25 February 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice stated that even if the CDPP had the initial intention of holding meetings with its supporters, those meetings later took on the character of demonstrations, marches, processions and picketing, which fall under the provisions of the Assemblies Act, and that the leaders of the CDPP were therefore required to comply with the provisions of the Assemblies Act.
The Christian Democratic People's Party (CDPP) appealed against the Supreme Court of Justice's ruling of 25 February 2002.
On 15 March 2002, the Supreme Court of Justice dismissed the CDPP's appeal against the ruling of 25 February 2002.
The Supreme Court of Justice's judgment of 25 February 2002 declaring the CDPP gatherings illegal became final on 15 March 2002.
In the course of the present proceedings before the Court, the Government submitted a video with images of gatherings held by CDPP deputies on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.
The gatherings shown in the video submitted by the Government were held in Great National Assembly Square, in a pedestrian area, in front of the government buildings.
The participants in the gatherings shown in the video appeared to number several hundred and included people of different ages varying from schoolchildren to pensioners.
According to the time displayed on the video images, the gatherings commenced at around 1 p.m. and lasted for about two hours.
During the gatherings shown in the video, different personalities made speeches critical of the ruling Communist Party, the government and its policy.
It appears from the video submitted by the Government that traffic was not disrupted as a result of the gatherings held on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.
No signs of violence can be seen in the video submitted by the Government of the gatherings held on 15, 16, 17 and 18 January 2002.
'The Layabout's Anthem' (Imnul Golanilor — a song that originated in the 1990 Bucharest student demonstrations) was played frequently at the gatherings shown in the video.

The chorus of 'The Layabout's Anthem' (Imnul Golanilor) included the following lines: 'I'd rather be a slacker than a traitor (Mai bine haimana, decât trădător) / I'd rather be a hooligan than a dictator (Mai bine huligan, decât dictator) / I'd rather be a layabout than an activist (Mai bine golan, decât activist) / I'd rather be dead than a communist (Mai bine mort, decât comunist).'
